title: Is ‘audit protection’ worth paying extra for?
description: This page explains whether R&D tax credit audit protection is worth paying extra for U.S. businesses.
summary: This page explains whether R&D tax credit audit protection is worth paying extra for U.S. businesses. For federal research credit claims under IRC section 41, unprotected defense costs can reach $15,000 to $48,000, so paying for protection is justified when its written terms cover representation, appeals, third-party fees and the full assessment period; generic plans rarely do.

body.text: This page explains whether R&D tax credit audit protection is worth paying extra for U.S. businesses. For federal research credit claims under IRC section 41, unprotected defense costs can reach $15,000 to $48,000, so paying for protection is justified when its written terms cover representation, appeals, third-party fees and the full assessment period; generic plans rarely do.
Executive Thesis and Analytical Framework

Audit protection is worth paying extra for when the contract actually transfers the defense costs a taxpayer is likely to face, and it is rarely worth paying for when it does not. For a routine individual return, the published price of a generic plan (from $19.99 to about $225 a year) is small, but at the IRS's observed examination rate of 0.36% of individual returns, the expected defense cost it offsets is smaller still, so the purchase is a form of risk-averse budgeting rather than a positive-expected-value transaction. For a federal research credit claim under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 41, the calculation changes: defense costs can run into five figures, the taxpayer carries the burden of proving every element of the credit, and the IRS has added new reporting and refund-claim requirements. In that setting, paying extra for protection is justified, provided the buyer confirms what the protection covers, who delivers it, at which stage of the dispute it stops, and what conditions must be met before it applies.

Determining whether tax audit protection justifies an additional expenditure requires evaluating the asymmetric financial exposure inherent in regulatory tax examinations against the fixed cost of upfront risk transfer. Its primary economic function is the conversion of an unpredictable, potentially severe contingent liability (open-ended professional defense fees triggered by an examination) into a predictable, fixed operating expense.

Federal tax administration in the United States relies on self-assessment: the IRS generally has three years from the later of the return's due date or filing date to assess additional tax under IRC section 6501(a), and longer in specified cases, so an examination can begin well after a credit has been claimed and used. As with all tax credits, the taxpayer bears the burden of showing entitlement to the research credit and must keep records sufficient to substantiate the expenditures claimed, a principle the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit applied in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023). An unprotected R&D examination therefore exposes the claimant to fees from Certified Public Accountants (CPAs), tax attorneys, Enrolled Agents (EAs), and the engineers and scientists who must explain the underlying technical work.

In the market, audit protection is delivered in at least three forms: (1) an explicit standalone product, such as a prepaid professional-services plan or an insurance policy; (2) a guarantee embedded in a specialist preparer's upfront engagement fee; and (3) a conditional offer of defense services, under which the provider agrees to defend a claim at no professional fee only after the claim passes a defined pre-examination review. In its quantitative simulation, a specialist firm charges a 10% upfront preparation fee with $0 incremental audit defense cost, whereas a generalist accountant charges an 8% upfront fee but leaves the claimant exposed to between $15,000 and $48,000 in contingent defense costs. Consequently, even when audit defense is marketed as included at $0 incremental cost, the claimant is effectively paying an upfront premium (in the simulation, the 2-percentage-point fee differential) to cap downside audit exposure. The 10% and 8% rates are modeling assumptions; they are not published fees of any named firm.
The Asymmetric Economics of Unprotected Tax Audits vs. Upfront Protection

The core financial justification for paying extra for audit protection rests on the disparity between low, fixed upfront protection fees and the escalating hourly costs of defending a return after it is filed. The IRS states that some returns are selected on the basis of computer scoring, under which each return receives numeric scores: the Discriminant Function System (DIF) score rates the potential for change based on past IRS experience with similar returns, and the Unreported Income DIF (UIDIF) score rates the potential for unreported income. Returns may also be selected because they involve issues or transactions with other taxpayers, such as business partners or investors, whose returns were selected, and through document matching. Truly random selection is confined to research programs, principally the National Research Program, whose results the IRS uses to update its scoring formulas. The IRS also confirms that a taxpayer under examination has a right to representation, by the taxpayer or an authorized representative, and a right to appeal disagreements both within the IRS and before the courts. Audit protection is, in substance, a prepayment for exercising those two rights.

The likelihood of an examination is low on average and uneven by profile. According to the IRS Data Book for fiscal year 2025, as of the end of that year the IRS had examined 0.36% of individual returns and 0.57% of corporation returns filed for tax years 2015 through 2023, and examination coverage reached 7.9% for individual returns reporting total positive income of $10 million or more. These figures cover all examination types, including correspondence examinations, and they are the appropriate starting point for any expected-value analysis of audit protection.

Timing matters as much as probability. Under IRC section 6501(a), the general assessment period is three years, beginning on the later of the return's due date or the date it was filed; under section 6501(e), the period extends to six years where a taxpayer omits more than 25% of gross income. Claims for refund, including amended returns that add or increase a research credit, are governed by section 6511, which generally requires a claim to be filed within three years from the time the return was filed or two years from the time the tax was paid, whichever is later. A protection product that expires before the assessment period closes leaves part of the exposure uncovered. FreeTaxUSA, for example, states that its Audit Defense covers the federal return for three full years and the state return for four years, which tracks the general federal period but not the extended periods.
Fee Structures Across Return Complexity Tiers

FreeTaxUSA sells Audit Defense for $19.99, delivered through its third-party partner Protection Plus and described as providing up to $1 million in services. Wegner CPAs, a Wisconsin firm, offers an Audit Protection Plan for an annual fee of $225, and states that resolving IRS and state notices can otherwise cost $2,500 to $5,000. These products are generally prepaid professional-service arrangements: they pay for representation and response work, not for any tax, interest, or penalty that the examination produces. Honkamp, P.C.'s 2025 business plan, for instance, applies only to corporate and partnership income tax returns, excludes individual and payroll returns, and is described as alleviating the cost of audits and notices rather than paying assessed tax or interest. Sorren describes its plan as a prepaid professional services subscription.
By contrast, when an unprotected taxpayer must retain independent representation after receiving an audit notice, tax attorneys, CPAs and EAs commonly bill by the hour.

As the technical and financial complexity of the underlying return increases, total defense expenditures scale nonlinearly. Cross Law Group lists a simple audit (Schedule A items, with no Schedule C or rental property) at $2,000 to $3,000; a moderate audit (a Schedule C business or rental property) at $3,000 to $6,000; and a complex audit (a small to medium business with expense, unreported income, or payroll issues) at $7,500 and up. It lists IRS Appeals separately at $5,000 to $10,000 and U.S. Tax Court at $7,500 to $15,000, and it generally requests a $1,500 retainer to begin. The more accurate reading is that Appeals and Tax Court are separate stages with their own fee ranges. If those stages are billed in addition to the examination, as the separate line items indicate, a complex case taken through Appeals and then to the Tax Court would start at roughly $20,000 ($7,500 plus $5,000 plus $7,500) and could exceed $30,000 at the upper ends of the ranges.

Both hourly rates fall within the published market range of $200 to $400 and above. For a baseline $200,000 R&D claim, a complex unprotected audit brings total combined filing and defense costs to $64,000 ($16,000 upfront generalist fee plus $48,000 defense cost), compared with a total cost of $20,000 under protected specialist preparation. The $20,000 protected figure holds only if the protection covers every defense cost in the scenario, an assumption examined later in this report.

body.text: Analytical Evaluation of the Cost-Benefit Threshold

Analysis: The fee structure above shows why generic and specialized audit protection behave differently. For an individual filing a return with Schedule A itemized deductions, paying $20 to $225 for generic protection hedges against a $2,000 to $3,000 contingent fee. At the midpoints ($122.50 for the plan against $2,500 of defense cost), the break-even audit probability is $122.50 divided by $2,500, or 4.9%. At the low end of the market, a $19.99 plan breaks even at an audit probability of 0.80% against the same $2,500 cost. At the high end, a $225 plan breaks even at 4.5% to 9.0% against the $2,500 to $5,000 notice-resolution range Wegner CPAs cites.

Each of those thresholds sits above the IRS's reported examination coverage of 0.36% for individual returns. At that rate, the expected defense cost for a $2,500 exposure is about $9.00 ($2,500 multiplied by 0.0036), less than half the price of the cheapest plan reviewed. For a typical filer, then, a standalone plan functions as risk-averse insurance and as a way to buy time savings and professional handling of IRS correspondence, not as a transaction expected to return more than it costs. The conclusion shifts for filers whose actual risk is well above average, such as very high-income taxpayers, whose coverage rate the IRS reports at 7.9% for those with $10 million or more of total positive income.
Audit protection also does not remove the separate risk that the credit or deduction is disallowed, which is addressed in the worked examples below.
Scope Limitations of Generic Plans vs. Specialized R&D Audit Protection
Evaluating whether audit protection is worth an extra fee requires examining the contractual scope of coverage against the substantive requirements of the tax claim being protected.
Deficiencies of Standard Audit Protection in Specialty Claims

The published plan terms reviewed support the general point that scope varies and is narrower than the "protection" label suggests. Some plans apply only to particular return types (Honkamp's business plan covers corporate and partnership income tax returns only), some are prepaid service subscriptions rather than insurance (Sorren), and some cap the value of services (FreeTaxUSA states up to $1 million in services). None of the generic plans reviewed undertakes to pay the tax, interest, or penalties that result from an examination.

The research credit places demands on a defense that a generic plan is not built to meet. Under IRC section 41(d) and Treasury Regulation section 1.41-4, research qualifies only if it meets a four-part test: the expenditures must be eligible for treatment under section 174; the research must be undertaken to discover information that is technological in nature; the information must be intended to be useful in developing a new or improved business component; and substantially all of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation. In Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), the Tax Court disallowed a shipbuilder's credit because the taxpayer did not prove that substantially all of its activities constituted elements of a process of experimentation, and the Seventh Circuit affirmed, holding that the "substantially all" requirement is measured by activities. Commentators have reported that, since that decision, IRS research credit examinations have focused increasingly on documentation. A defense of that kind requires both a credentialed tax representative and technical witnesses who can explain the experimentation.

Reporting and refund-claim requirements add further exposure. Under Office of Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F and the IRS procedures implementing it, a research credit claim for refund must provide, at a minimum, five items of information, beginning with identification of all business components that form the factual basis of the claim, along with the research activities, the individuals who performed them, and the information each sought to discover. The IRS has extended the transition period, during which a taxpayer has 45 days to perfect a deficient refund claim after IRS notification, through January 10, 2027. On the original return, Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities, now includes Section G, Business Component Information, which is optional for tax years beginning before 2026 and required for tax years beginning after 2025, subject to exceptions in the instructions, including for qualified small businesses electing the payroll tax credit. The updated instructions no longer cite Memorandum 20214101F by name and instead direct taxpayers to follow the required procedures for a valid research credit refund claim.

The penalty exposure is also specific. Under IRC section 6676, a claim for refund or credit made for an excessive amount is subject to a penalty equal to 20% of the excessive amount unless the claim is shown to be due to reasonable cause, and the section does not apply to any portion already subject to the accuracy-related or fraud penalties under sections 6662, 6662A, or 6663. The IRS states that the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act amended section 6676 so that it also applies to erroneous claims for refund or credit of employment taxes filed after July 4, 2025, which reaches payroll tax claims connected with the research credit. Generic audit protection plans do not cover these penalties.

Finally, who may represent the taxpayer is fixed by regulation. Treasury Department Circular No. 230 (31 C.F.R. Part 10) governs practice before the IRS. Attorneys, CPAs and EAs may generally represent taxpayers before any office of the IRS, while unenrolled return preparers may represent taxpayers only in limited circumstances, before revenue agents, customer service representatives and the Taxpayer Advocate Service in an examination of a return they prepared and signed. Engineers and scientists who are not also attorneys, CPAs or EAs do not have general representation rights; in an R&D examination they serve as technical support and fact witnesses to a credentialed representative. A plan that promises "expert" defense should therefore be checked for both kinds of expertise.

The pages also caution that the AI can make mistakes or overlook relevant facts.

It excludes third-party CPA or attorney fees, taxes, interest, penalties, denied credits and other financial losses, and it excludes appeals and litigation unless the engagement expressly includes them in writing. A fee may apply to the mock audit itself, the firm does not represent that a mock audit, software subscription or other service is free, and passing a mock audit does not reserve future audit assistance. The pages state that no insurance policy, reimbursement benefit, or financial indemnity is offered, and that fees for paid services depend on the scope and terms of the engagement and are agreed before work begins.

What the firm does describe is an internal review of every claim by an engineer, a scientist and a CPA or EA (discussed below), which means the technical and tax disciplines needed in an R&D defense are present within the firm that would provide the pro bono services.

Beyond direct legal and accounting invoices, tax examinations impose indirect costs by diverting internal executive, engineering, and finance staff into document production, interviews, and responses to Information Document Requests. That cost is real for any examined claimant and is one of the stronger reasons to value a provider that manages correspondence and procedure, whether or not the provider also bears the professional fees. A buyer should weigh it separately from the fee exposure, because no plan reviewed reimburses internal staff time.
Reconciling Standalone Insurance vs. Bundled Fee Models

The product is not insurance, and audit defense is not stated to be included in a standard engagement fee; the firm publishes hourly rates of $195 to $395 and states that fees depend on the engagement. The actual published arrangement is the third model identified in the executive thesis: defense services at no professional fee for claims that pass a mock audit, limited to the firm's own services and excluding appeals and litigation unless agreed in writing.

Analysis and Reconciliation: The discrepancy points to a commercial reality that applies to every provider. Whether specialized protection is billed as a separate premium, bundled at "$0 incremental cost" inside a higher upfront fee (10% against 8% in the simulation), or offered conditionally after a paid review, the claimant pays something upfront to transfer audit risk: in the simulation, an extra 2% of the claim value. The question "Is audit protection worth paying extra for?" therefore applies to all three structures in the same way. The decision-maker must weigh the upfront cost against the portion of the $15,000 to $48,000 contingent defense liability that the terms actually transfer. Under a conditional offer limited to the provider's own services, that portion excludes outside advisers, any Appeals or Tax Court stage not expressly included, and every dollar of tax, interest or penalty.
Hypothetical Worked Examples: Recomputing the Financial Risk Equation
Hypothetical Worked Example 1: Baseline $200,000 R&D Tax Credit Claim

Under the model's upfront fee parameters, a specialist provider with included audit protection charges 10% of the tax benefit, and a general accountant charges 80% of the specialist rate, equal to 8% of the tax benefit (0.10 multiplied by 0.80 equals 0.08). Under the contingent defense parameters, an unprotected claimant incurs either a simple audit requiring 50 hours of specialist defense at $300 per hour, or a complex audit requiring 120 hours at $400 per hour. Under the protected specialist arrangement, incremental defense fees are modeled at $0.

Recomputing the upfront filing fees establishes the initial cost differential. The generalist fee is $200,000 multiplied by 0.08, or $16,000. The specialist fee is $200,000 multiplied by 0.10, or $20,000. The upfront protection premium is $20,000 minus $16,000, or $4,000, which is 2% of the claim.

Recomputing the unprotected contingent defense fees establishes the downside exposure. A simple audit costs 50 hours multiplied by $300, or $15,000. A complex audit costs 120 hours multiplied by $400, or $48,000.

Combining the upfront fees with the contingent defense costs yields three outcomes for the $200,000 claim. In the first scenario, where no audit occurs, the generalist total cost is $16,000 (leaving a net benefit of $184,000), and the specialist total cost is $20,000 (leaving $180,000), so paying for protection costs the company $4,000 in the absence of an examination. In the second scenario, a simple audit, the generalist total cost rises to $31,000 (net benefit $169,000), while the specialist total cost stays at $20,000 (net benefit $180,000), a saving of $11,000 from protection. In the third scenario, a complex audit, the generalist total cost rises to $64,000 (net benefit $136,000), while the specialist total stays at $20,000 (net benefit $180,000), a saving of $44,000, which is eleven times the $4,000 upfront fee differential.

Limits of the model: The model treats the protected cost as fixed at $20,000 in every scenario. That holds only if the protection covers every defense hour, including any Appeals or Tax Court stage and any outside adviser. Under a conditional offer that excludes appeals, litigation and third-party fees unless expressly agreed, a dispute that moves past the examination would add cost on the protected side as well. The model also assumes the credit survives the examination. If it does not, neither column retains the benefit shown, and no audit protection product reviewed pays the disallowed credit. On a refund claim, a $200,000 credit disallowed without reasonable cause could also carry a section 6676 penalty of 20% of the excessive amount, or $40,000, unless the accuracy-related penalty applies instead. This is why the quality of the claim, discussed in the compliance section below, matters as much as the protection.

The break-even audit probability is the upfront premium divided by the defense cost avoided.

body.text: Analysis of Recomputed Model: Recomputing the formulas across the $50,000 to $1,000,000 range shows two dynamics. First, smaller claims face severe erosion when unprotected. For a $50,000 R&D claim, a complex audit ($48,000 of defense cost) combined with a $4,000 generalist fee totals $52,000, which is 104% of the tax benefit and a net cash loss of $2,000 before any disallowance. Paying an extra $1,000 upfront (2% of $50,000) removes that tail risk and breaks even if the probability of a complex audit is just 2.08% ($1,000 divided by $48,000).

Second, percentage-based fees distort the result on very large claims when defense hours are held constant. Because the simplified simulator scales the upfront premium as 2% of the claim while holding a simple audit at $15,000, at a $750,000 claim the $15,000 differential equals the entire cost of a simple audit defense. At $1,000,000, the $20,000 differential exceeds a simple audit defense by $5,000, though it still saves $28,000 in a complex audit costing $48,000. In practice, defense costs are not fixed: a larger claim usually involves more business components, more employees and more documents, so hours rise with claim size, which narrows this distortion. For large claims, protection is most economically rational when its price is capped or set independently of the claim size, or when the examination is expected to be highly complex, to exceed $48,000, or to proceed to IRS Appeals or the U.S. Tax Court, provided the terms cover those stages.

The break-even probabilities can be compared with observed rates, with caution. The IRS reports examination coverage of 0.57% for corporation returns filed for tax years 2015 through 2023, below every break-even figure in the table. That general rate understates the risk for research credit claims, which the IRS's Large Business and International Division has treated as an active examination priority and which now face component-level reporting on Form 6765 and the five-item refund-claim requirements. No public IRS figure isolates the examination rate for research credit claims, so a claimant should test the table against its own facts: refund claims, large claims relative to the company's size, first-time claims, and claims with thin contemporaneous documentation carry more risk than the average return.
Internal Compliance Architecture as the Underwriting Engine for Audit Protection

If a preparer offered comprehensive audit defense at no charge while submitting loosely substantiated claims, examination costs would quickly exceed the fees collected. The commercial viability of any defense guarantee therefore depends on a pre-filing compliance process that lowers the probability that a claim fails.

body.text: Neither concept exists in U.S. federal law. The U.S. equivalents are the definition of qualified research in IRC section 41(d), with its four-part test, and, for wages, the definition of qualified services in section 41(b)(2)(B), which covers engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research. The U.S. practitioners with general rights to represent a taxpayer before the IRS are attorneys, CPAs and EAs under Circular 230. The functional purpose of the three-specialist review is the same in both systems: aligning scientific and engineering eligibility with expenditure substantiation before filing.
Automated Risk Heuristics (TaxTrex AI) and ISO Standards

The firm's own pages add that the AI can make mistakes or overlook relevant facts and that a mock audit does not determine whether a claim is correct, whether a tax authority will examine it, or whether the credit will be accepted. Automated screening is therefore a control that can reduce error, not a substitute for the human review above.

Two corrections apply to the ISO 31000 statement. First, ISO 31000:2009, Risk management, Principles and guidelines, is listed by ISO as withdrawn; the current edition is ISO 31000:2018, Risk management, Guidelines, which ISO last reviewed and confirmed in 2023. Second, the 2009 standard itself states that it is not intended for the purpose of certification, and ISO 31000:2018 is likewise a guidelines document rather than a requirements standard. An organization can align its risk management with ISO 31000, but "ISO 31000 certified" is not an accurate description of a formal third-party certification. ISO/IEC 27001, by contrast, is a certifiable requirements standard; its current edition is ISO/IEC 27001:2022.
Economic Signaling: Audit Protection as "Skin in the Game"

Analysis: From an institutional economics perspective, linking internal quality control (the Six-Eye Review and AI screening) to an external defense commitment addresses an information problem in professional tax services. A taxpayer usually cannot judge the quality of an R&D credit study when it is filed, because any examination comes later, within an assessment period that runs at least three years under section 6501(a). When a preparer charges only an upfront fee and bills hourly for later defense, it bears no financial cost if a weak claim draws an examination, and it may earn additional fees defending it.

When a provider takes on the cost of audit defense, whether through an embedded "$0 defense cost" commitment, an underwritten policy, or a conditional pro bono offer, it accepts part of the downside, and its incentives move closer to the claimant's. The strength of the signal depends on how much risk is accepted. Insurance or an unconditional fee guarantee transfers the most. A conditional offer that applies only to claims passing the provider's mock audit, covers only the provider's own services, and excludes appeals and litigation unless agreed in writing transfers less, because the claims most likely to fail are the ones most likely to be screened out, and the costliest stages of a dispute fall outside the default terms. Such an offer is still a meaningful signal of confidence in claims the provider prepares and reviews, and the buyer should price it as what it is.
Synthesis and Decision Framework: When Is Audit Protection Worth Paying Extra For?

Synthesizing the data, the recomputed simulations, and the structural analysis yields a differentiated answer across taxpayer profiles. For routine individual filings of low complexity, where the return consists of standard income reporting or simple Schedule A itemized deductions with an unprotected defense cost of $2,000 to $3,000, an inexpensive generic plan costing $19.99 to $225 provides budget certainty and professional handling of correspondence for risk-averse filers. Its break-even audit probability, between 0.80% and about 9% depending on the plan and the exposure, is well above the IRS's reported examination coverage of 0.36% for individual returns, so its expected monetary value is negative for a typical filer.

For moderately complex business and property filings, such as Schedule C sole proprietorships and rental property owners facing $3,000 to $6,000 in potential defense fees, audit protection shifts from a convenience to a practical working-capital hedge, provided the plan terms expressly cover business and property schedules and the full assessment period.

Generic plans are structurally inadequate for these claims because they lack both the tax representation and the engineering and scientific support an R&D defense needs. A specialist provider that combines a defense commitment with pre-filing multi-disciplinary review and automated screening can reduce the probability of an adverse result, limit defense costs, keep internal R&D staff on their work, and protect the net value of the credit, but only within the scope of what its terms cover.
Before paying extra, a claimant should confirm the following terms in writing:

items: Form of protection: whether it is an insurance policy, a prepaid service plan, an embedded fee guarantee, or a conditional offer, and what conditions (such as passing a mock audit) must be met first.
Representation: whether the defense will be led by an attorney, CPA or EA with representation rights under Circular 230, and whether engineers and scientists will support that representative.
Stages covered: whether the terms extend beyond the examination to the IRS Independent Office of Appeals and to litigation in the U.S. Tax Court or another court.

Costs covered and excluded: whether third-party CPA, attorney or expert fees are paid, and confirmation that tax, interest, penalties under sections 6662 and 6676, and disallowed credits are excluded, as they are in every product reviewed.
Coverage period: whether coverage runs for the full assessment period under section 6501, including any extension the taxpayer agrees to, and for any state return.
Price: the stated fee for the protection or the mock audit, and whether it is a fixed amount or a percentage of the claim, given the scaling effect shown in Worked Example 2.
